section.title: Driving Out the Nations
section.sectionRationale: This chapter contains the severe command to devote the Canaanite nations to destruction, language bound tightly to a specific, unrepeatable moment in redemptive history when Israel functioned as God's chosen instrument of judgment on centuries of accumulated wickedness; it must be read with interpretive honesty, never as a warrant for violence in any later era.
section.thesis: Because the LORD chose Israel not for any greatness of their own but purely out of love and covenant faithfulness, He commands them to devote the Canaanite nations and their idols to complete destruction, a description of a bounded moment in redemptive history that anticipates final judgment on all evil and the spiritual warfare of the new covenant, never a warrant for violence today.
section.frameNote: Five movements: the command to devote the nations to destruction; Israel chosen not for size but for love; the blessing that follows obedience; the call not to fear the nations, remembering Egypt; and the warning to burn the idols and refuse their silver and gold.

units.label: Devote them to complete destruction
units.note: make no treaty, show no mercy

verses.text: When the LORD your God brings you into the land that you are entering to possess, and He drives out before you many nations, the Hittites, Girgashites, Amorites, Canaanites, Perizzites, Hivites, and Jebusites, seven nations larger and stronger than you,
and when the LORD your God has delivered them over to you to defeat them, then you must {{cherem|devote}} them to complete destruction. Make no treaty with them and show them no mercy.
Do not intermarry with them. Do not give your daughters to their sons or take their daughters for your sons,
because they will turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods. Then the anger of the LORD will burn against you, and He will swiftly destroy you.
Instead, this is what you are to do to them: tear down their altars, smash their sacred pillars, cut down their Asherah poles, and burn their idols in the fire.

units.label: A holy people, chosen not for size but for love

verses.text: For you are a people {{qadosh|holy}} to the LORD your God. The LORD your God has chosen you to be a people for His {{segullah|prized possession}} out of all peoples on the face of the earth.
The LORD did not set His affection on you and choose you because you were more numerous than the other peoples, for you were the fewest of all peoples.
But because the LORD loved you and kept the oath He swore to your fathers, He brought you out with a mighty hand and redeemed you from the house of slavery, from the hand of Pharaoh king of Egypt.
Know therefore that the LORD your God is God, the faithful God who keeps His covenant of {{chesed|loving devotion}} for a thousand generations of those who love Him and keep His commandments.
But those who hate Him He repays to their faces with destruction; He will not hesitate to repay to his face the one who hates Him.
So keep the commandments and statutes and ordinances that I am giving you to follow this day.
If you listen to these ordinances and keep them carefully, then the LORD your God will keep His covenant and the loving devotion that He swore to your fathers.

He will love you and bless you and multiply you. He will bless the fruit of your womb and the produce of your land, your grain, new wine, and oil, the young of your herds and the lambs of your flocks, in the land that He swore to your fathers to give you.
You will be blessed above all peoples; among you there will be no barren man or woman or livestock.
And the LORD will remove from you all sickness. He will not lay upon you any of the terrible diseases you knew in Egypt, but He will inflict them on all who hate you.
You must destroy all the peoples the LORD your God will deliver to you. Do not look on them with pity. Do not worship their gods, for that will be a snare to you.

units.label: Do not fear them: remember Egypt

verses.text: You may say in your heart, “These nations are greater than we are; how can we drive them out?”
But do not be afraid of them. Be sure to remember what the LORD your God did to Pharaoh and all Egypt:

the great trials that you saw, the signs and wonders, and the mighty hand and outstretched arm by which the LORD your God brought you out. The LORD your God will do the same to all the peoples you now fear.
Moreover, the LORD your God will send the hornet against them until even the survivors hiding from you have perished.
Do not be terrified by them, for the LORD your God, who is among you, is a great and awesome God.
The LORD your God will drive out these nations before you little by little. You will not be enabled to eliminate them all at once, or the wild animals would multiply around you.
But the LORD your God will give them over to you and throw them into great confusion, until they are destroyed.
He will hand their kings over to you, and you will wipe out their names from under heaven. No one will be able to stand against you; you will annihilate them.

units.label: Burn the idols; do not covet

verses.text: You must burn up the images of their gods; do not covet the silver and gold that is on them or take it for yourselves, or you will be ensnared by it; for it is detestable to the LORD your God.
And you must not bring any detestable thing into your house, or you, like it, will be set apart for destruction. You are to utterly detest and abhor it, because it is set apart for destruction.

cherem.gloss: To devote irrevocably to destruction, setting something apart entirely for the LORD by destroying it, so nothing of it may be kept for personal gain. It describes a specific, bounded act of divine judgment carried out through Israel at this stage of redemptive history, not a general rule of warfare.

qadosh.gloss: Holy, set apart. Israel's holiness here is a status given by God's choice, not earned by merit or size; it grounds the call to be different from the surrounding nations, especially in worship.

segullah.gloss: A treasured, personal possession, often used of a king's private treasure. Applied to Israel, it expresses God's intimate, valuing love for His people, later applied to the church, 1 Peter 2:9.

chesed.gloss: Loving devotion, steadfast covenant loyalty. Combines love and faithfulness in a single word, describing God's unwavering commitment to keep His covenant promises across generations, grounded in His own character rather than in Israel's merit.

basic.context: Moses commands Israel to devote the Canaanite nations and their idols to complete destruction as they enter the land, grounding this severe instruction not in Israel's own greatness but in God's covenant love and faithfulness to the promise He swore to their fathers.
basic.hermeneutics: This is one of the hardest passages in Deuteronomy, and it deserves honesty: it describes a specific, bounded act of divine judgment carried out through Israel at a unique moment in redemptive history, ending centuries of accumulated Canaanite wickedness, Genesis 15:16, not a timeless rule for how any nation or individual should treat others. The New Testament redirects God's people entirely away from national conquest toward spiritual warfare against sin and evil, and toward advancing Christ's kingdom by the gospel, not the sword.
basic.originalLanguages: Cherem, devote to destruction, describes an act set irrevocably apart for God, forbidding any personal profit from it. Israel is qadosh, holy, and segullah, a treasured possession, chosen purely by God's chesed, His loving, faithful devotion, not by their size or merit.
basic.typology: The devoted destruction of Canaanite idolatry anticipates the final, complete judgment of all evil at the end of the age, and Israel's calling as a treasured possession chosen by grace anticipates the church, gathered from every nation purely by God's mercy, 1 Peter 2:9-10.
basic.christ: This chapter's severity belongs to Israel's unique role as a national, political body carrying out God's specific judgment in that era; the New Testament redirects believers to spiritual warfare, not against flesh and blood, but against evil itself, Ephesians 6:12, since Christ's kingdom advances by gospel proclamation, not by the sword, John 18:36. The certain final judgment on all evil, which this chapter foreshadows in miniature, is entrusted entirely to Christ, the righteous judge.
basic.god: God is holy and will not tolerate idolatry, yet the driving motive behind this whole chapter is His covenant love, chesed, freely set on Israel not because of their merit but because He loved them and kept His ancient oath, showing that even His severest commands in this passage flow from faithful, covenant love rather than caprice.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 15:16 explains that Canaan's judgment awaited the completion of the Amorites' iniquity, showing this was a judgment on real accumulated wickedness, not ethnic hostility. Ephesians 6:12 redirects the church's warfare to spiritual powers, not human enemies. 1 Peter 2:9-10 applies Israel's identity as a treasured, holy people to the church.
basic.oneStory: This chapter names Israel's calling in stark, severe terms bound to a specific moment in redemptive history, while revealing that even here, God's motive is covenant love, not caprice. The New Testament fulfills its deeper pattern, final judgment on all evil and a people treasured purely by grace, in Christ, who conquers not with the sword but through the cross, and who gathers His treasured people from every nation by His Spirit.

context.literary:
Chapter 7 is the first extended application of the Shema. Deuteronomy 6:14 had said, 'Do not follow other gods, the gods of the peoples around you'; chapter 7 now names those peoples and says what exclusive love for the LORD will require when Israel meets them. The first and second commands of Deuteronomy 5:7-9 stand behind every paragraph.

The chapter is carefully arranged. Its two outer sections, verses 1 to 5 and 16 to 26, deal with the nations and their gods; both end with the destruction of idols, verses 5 and 25 to 26. The centre, verses 6 to 15, turns from what Israel must do to who Israel is and who God is: a holy people, chosen out of love, verses 6 to 8, the faithful God who keeps covenant, verses 9 to 11, and the blessings that follow obedience, verses 12 to 15. The severity of the frame rests on the grace of the centre. Moses will not let Israel hear the command without first hearing why they were chosen.

Several words tie the chapter together. 'Snare' appears in verse 16 and verse 25; the danger in both is not military but religious, the pull of other gods and their silver and gold. 'Love' runs through the centre: the LORD loved you, verse 8; He keeps covenant with those who love Him, verse 9; He will love you, verse 13. 'Hate' is its counterpart: those who hate Him are repaid, verse 10, and diseases fall on all who hate Israel, verse 15.

The chapter also anticipates Israel's fear, a pattern familiar from Deuteronomy 1:28, where the spies' report had melted their hearts. Verse 17 quotes what Israel may say in their heart, and verses 18 to 24 answer by memory: remember Pharaoh. The closing verses then turn back on Israel itself. A detestable thing brought home would make Israel 'like it,' set apart for destruction, verse 26. The same judgment could fall on the chosen people.
context.historical:
The seven nations of verse 1 are a stylised list. Other passages give six, Exodus 3:8, or ten, Genesis 15:19-21, and seven here expresses completeness: the whole population of the land. The Hittites mentioned are probably groups in Canaan connected in some way with the northern empire of that name; the Amorites and Canaanites are broad terms for the peoples of the hill country and the coast; the Jebusites held Jerusalem until David, 2 Samuel 5:6-7. In the Late Bronze Age Canaan was a patchwork of small walled city states, each with its king, which fits the promise of verse 24, 'He will hand their kings over to you.'

The religious objects of verse 5 are known from archaeology and from texts found at Ugarit on the Syrian coast. Altars were for sacrifice to Baal and other gods. 'Sacred pillars' were standing stones set up at shrines. 'Asherah poles' were wooden cult objects associated with the goddess Asherah, a consort figure in Canaanite religion. Deuteronomy links these cults with practices the LORD calls detestable, including burning sons and daughters in sacrifice, Deuteronomy 12:31 and 18:10, and the sexual practices of Leviticus 18:24-25, where the land itself 'will vomit out its inhabitants.'

The practice of devoting a city to a god by destruction was not unique to Israel. The Moabite king Mesha, on a stone inscription from the ninth century BC, boasts that he devoted an Israelite town to his god Kemosh, using the same word. What is distinctive in Deuteronomy is the reason given and the limit set. The command applies to these peoples in this land, in the context of God's long delayed judgment, Genesis 15:16 and Deuteronomy 9:4-5, and Israel's gain is explicitly forbidden: the silver and gold of the idols must be burned, verse 25.

The precedent the first hearers knew was recent. East of the Jordan they had fought Sihon and Og, and Deuteronomy 2:34 and 3:6 describe those cities devoted to destruction. The command of chapter 7 extends that experience to the land west of the river.
context.canonical:
The chapter develops earlier instructions in Exodus. Exodus 23:23-33 already promised the hornet, the gradual driving out, 'Little by little I will drive them out ahead of you,' Exodus 23:30, and the warning that their gods would be a snare, Exodus 23:33. Exodus 34:12-16 forbids treaties and intermarriage for the same reason. Deuteronomy 20:16-18 later restates the command and gives its purpose: 'so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.'

The following books show both the command and its failure. Jericho is devoted to destruction, but Rahab and her household are spared because she sheltered the spies, Joshua 6:17 and 6:25. Achan covets the devoted silver and gold and brings the ban on himself, Joshua 7:1 and 7:21, exactly as verses 25 and 26 warned. The Gibeonites trick Israel into a treaty, Joshua 9:15. Judges 1:27-28 and 2:1-3 record that the nations were not driven out and became thorns and snares. Solomon's foreign wives 'turned his heart after other gods,' 1 Kings 11:4, citing this very prohibition. At last Israel itself went into exile because it 'walked in the customs of the nations that the LORD had driven out,' 2 Kings 17:8.

The prophets widen the horizon. Isaiah 34:2 speaks of the LORD devoting all nations to destruction, and the Old Testament's last verse warns that God may 'strike the land with a curse,' Malachi 4:6, with the same word. Zechariah 14:11 promises that 'never again will there be an utter destruction,' and Revelation 22:3 echoes it: 'No longer will there be any curse.' In the New Testament, the language of chosen, holy and treasured people passes to the church, 1 Peter 2:9-10 and Titus 2:14, and Rahab is named among the faithful, Hebrews 11:31, and in the line of Jesus, Matthew 1:5.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Moses' first concern is Israel's worship. Every reason he gives for the command concerns other gods: intermarriage will 'turn your sons away from following Me to serve other gods,' verse 4; the idols must be burned, verse 5; their gods 'will be a snare,' verse 16; the silver and gold are 'detestable,' verse 25. The chapter is about removing a rival religion from the land God is giving, so that Israel can love Him with an undivided heart, Deuteronomy 6:5.

His second concern is Israel's self understanding. He wanted them to know they were not entering the land because they were strong, numerous or righteous. Verses 7 and 8 insist they were 'the fewest of all peoples' and were chosen only because the LORD loved them and kept His oath. Deuteronomy 9:4-5 adds that it is not because of their righteousness but because of the nations' wickedness. Israel is the instrument of judgment, not its reason.

His third concern is their courage. A people who feared giants and walled cities once before, Deuteronomy 1:28, needed to remember Egypt, verses 18 and 19, and trust that the LORD among them was 'a great and awesome God,' verse 21. Finally, Moses meant them to feel the warning that the same holiness applied to them. If they adopted the idols, the anger of the LORD would burn against them, verse 4, and they would become devoted to destruction, verse 26.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
This chapter is prescriptive for Israel at one moment: the entry into Canaan, under the leadership of God's appointed servants, against named peoples whose judgment had been foretold centuries earlier, Genesis 15:16. It is not a general law of war even within the Old Testament; Deuteronomy 20:10-15 gives different rules for distant cities. It gives no warrant to any later nation, church or person to take up the sword in God's name. Jesus rebuked His disciples when they wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Luke 9:54-55, and He declared that His kingdom is not of this world, John 18:36.

What does carry forward is the spiritual principle. Believers are to be decisive with idols in their own lives: 'flee from idolatry,' 1 Corinthians 10:14, 'keep yourselves from idols,' 1 John 5:21. The Ephesians who burned their magic books, Acts 19:19, show what verse 25 looks like under the new covenant. The warning against partnerships that pull the heart from God is restated in 2 Corinthians 6:14-16. Believers also hear the call to love enemies, Matthew 5:44, and to leave vengeance to God, Romans 12:19, trusting that final judgment belongs to Christ alone, Acts 17:31.

debates.question: How should Christians read the command to 'devote them to complete destruction' and 'show no mercy' toward the Canaanite nations?

views.label: Bounded, unrepeatable judgment
views.case: The command belongs to a unique moment in which God used Israel to carry out a judgment He had delayed for four generations, Genesis 15:16, on practices including child sacrifice, Deuteronomy 12:31. The same God later judged Israel by other nations for the same sins, 2 Kings 17:7-8, so the judgment was moral, not favouritism. No such mandate exists after Christ, whose kingdom advances by the gospel, John 18:36.

views.label: Stylised language of total victory
views.case: Many point out that ancient war reports often used sweeping language. The chapter itself forbids intermarriage, verse 3, and speaks of driving the nations out 'little by little,' verse 22, which assumes survivors. Joshua 10:40 says Joshua left no survivors, yet Joshua 11:22 and Judges 1:27-28 show that many remained. On this reading the stress falls on destroying the religious system and breaking the nations' hold on the land.

views.label: A hard text to face with humility
views.case: Others stress that even with these observations the command includes women and children, as Deuteronomy 2:34 records, and remains morally troubling. They counsel honest lament rather than quick solutions, while still affirming God's justice and refusing to treat the text as a model for any people today.

debates.bearing: The views are not exclusive. The text should be read with its own limits, its own rhetoric, and its own theological reasons, and never used to justify violence against any people. Its forward pointing meaning is the final judgment, which God entrusts to Christ, Acts 17:31, and the church's warfare is against spiritual evil, Ephesians 6:12.

debates.question: Was the command about ethnicity or about religion?

views.label: Religious, not ethnic
views.case: Every reason in the chapter concerns other gods, verses 4, 5, 16 and 25. Rahab the Canaanite was spared when she trusted the God of Israel, Joshua 6:25, and entered the line of David, Matthew 1:5. Ruth the Moabite joined Israel by confessing 'your God will be my God,' Ruth 1:16. And Israel itself would be treated like the nations if it served their gods, verse 26 and Deuteronomy 8:19-20.

views.label: A people and a land bound together
views.case: Others note that the command does name specific peoples, verse 1, and that later texts such as Ezra 9:1-2 treated separation from them as a matter of 'the holy seed.' In the ancient world religion and peoplehood were closely joined, so separation from a people's gods meant separation from the people as a community.

debates.bearing: The chapter's own logic is religious: the danger is the turning of the heart. The Rahab and Ruth stories show that the door was open to any outsider who turned to the LORD, and the New Testament makes that open door the heart of the gospel, Ephesians 2:12-13.

debates.question: What was the hornet of verse 20?

views.label: Literal insects
views.case: The word appears also in Exodus 23:28 and Joshua 24:12 as something God sends ahead of Israel. It may describe actual swarms that drove people from hiding, as verse 20 says, 'until even the survivors hiding from you have perished.'

views.label: A figure for panic
views.case: Exodus 23:27, the verse just before the hornet, says, 'I will send My terror ahead of you and throw into confusion every nation,' and Deuteronomy 7:23 speaks of 'great confusion.' The hornet may be a vivid image of God given dread that sent the enemy fleeing.

debates.bearing: Either way, Joshua 24:12 draws the point: 'not by your own sword or bow.' The victory belongs to God, which is why Israel must not fear the nations and must not boast over them.

study.originalLanguages:
Four words in this chapter repay closer attention, alongside the ones the basic text names.

The first is chashaq in verse 7, 'set His affection.' It is a strong, even passionate word. It describes Shechem's longing for Dinah in Genesis 34:8 and a man's desire for a woman taken captive in Deuteronomy 21:11. Moses uses it of God's attachment to Israel here and in Deuteronomy 10:15, 'the LORD has set His affection on your fathers and loved them.' The choice of word shows that election is not a cold decree. God's choosing of Israel is described in the language of a lover's heart.

The second is the verb 'redeemed' in verse 8, padah. It belongs to the world of ransom, the payment that releases a person or animal from another's claim; the firstborn of Israel had to be redeemed by a price. Deuteronomy uses it repeatedly of the exodus, Deuteronomy 9:26, 13:5 and 15:15, always with 'the house of slavery' or Egypt nearby. Israel's election and Israel's redemption are two sides of one act of love.

The third is the title in verse 9, 'the faithful God,' ha-el ha-neeman. Neeman comes from the root aman, to be firm or reliable, the root behind 'amen.' God is the one who can be leaned on, who holds firm to His covenant 'for a thousand generations.' The counterpart in verse 10 is striking: He repays those who hate Him 'to their faces,' el panav, a phrase repeated twice for emphasis. His faithfulness to those who love Him and His justice toward those who hate Him are equally personal.

The fourth cluster is the vocabulary of revulsion in verses 25 and 26. The idols are toevah, 'detestable,' a word Deuteronomy uses for what is abhorrent to God in worship and conduct, including the practices of Deuteronomy 12:31. Verse 26 then doubles its verbs in the Hebrew intensive construction, literally 'detesting you shall detest it and abhorring you shall abhor it,' rendered 'utterly detest and abhor.' The same verse uses cherem twice more, as the BSB footnote notes, and applies it to Israel: take the thing home and 'you, like it, will be set apart.' Verse 25 also warns, 'do not covet the silver and gold,' using chamad, the verb of the tenth commandment, Deuteronomy 5:21. Achan's confession in Joshua 7:21, 'I coveted them and took them,' uses the same verb.

The Septuagint renders segullah, 'prized possession' in verse 6, with laos periousios, 'a special people.' Paul uses the same Greek phrase in Titus 2:14 when he says Christ gave Himself 'to purify for Himself a people for His own possession.' The language of Deuteronomy 7:6 passes directly into the New Testament's description of the church.

typology.type: The devoted destruction of Canaanite idolatry
typology.fulfillment: The judgment of Canaan was a limited, historical anticipation of the final judgment of evil. The prophets widen it: Isaiah 34:2 speaks of the LORD devoting all nations to destruction. The New Testament places that final act entirely in Christ's hands. He judges with righteousness, Revelation 19:11, and God has fixed a day when He will judge the world by the Man He has appointed, Acts 17:30-31. The type falls far short, because Israel's warfare was carried out by sinful people and was partial and incomplete, Judges 1:27-28. The final judgment will be perfectly just, and it is preceded by a universal call to repent.

typology.type: Israel chosen as a treasured possession purely by grace
typology.fulfillment: Israel was chosen not for size or merit but because the LORD loved them, verses 7 and 8. The same pattern shapes the church. Paul reminds the Corinthians that not many of them were wise or powerful, since God chose the weak 'so that no one may boast,' 1 Corinthians 1:26-29. Peter applies Israel's titles directly to believers, 'a chosen people ... a holy nation, a people for God's own possession,' 1 Peter 2:9-10, and Titus 2:14 says Christ gave Himself to purify such a people. The escalation is in breadth: the treasured people now come from every nation.

typology.type: Rahab, the Canaanite spared from the ban
typology.fulfillment: Rahab belonged to the peoples of verse 1 and lived in the first city devoted to destruction, yet she and her household were spared because she received Israel's spies and trusted Israel's God, Joshua 6:25. She shows that the command was never ethnic hatred: the ban could be escaped by faith. The New Testament celebrates her in Hebrews 11:31 and James 2:25, and Matthew 1:5 places her in the genealogy of Jesus. In Christ this exception becomes the rule, as those once 'strangers to the covenants of the promise' are brought near through His blood, Ephesians 2:12-13.

Israel was to tear down altars, smash pillars and burn images, verse 5. Under the new covenant the enemy is the same, false worship, but the weapons change. Paul says believers do not wage war according to the flesh; their weapons 'have divine power to demolish strongholds,' tearing down arguments set up against the knowledge of God, 2 Corinthians 10:3-5. The Ephesian believers burned their own books of magic, Acts 19:19. The struggle is 'not against flesh and blood,' Ephesians 6:12. The type is transformed: the church fights idols by truth and repentance, never by force against people.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ first by showing, in the most severe terms, that God's judgment on evil is real. The Canaanites were not destroyed at random; Genesis 15:16 said their iniquity was not yet complete, and Deuteronomy 9:5 says the nations were driven out 'because of their wickedness.' Scripture does not treat this as a pattern for human action but as a preview of a judgment God reserves to Himself. The New Testament gives that judgment to Christ. Paul tells the Athenians that God has set a day 'when He will judge the world with justice by the Man He has appointed,' Acts 17:31, and describes the Lord Jesus revealed from heaven 'in blazing fire,' 2 Thessalonians 1:7-8. The One who judges is also the One who first calls all people everywhere to repent, Acts 17:30.

It leads to Christ by the way it treats Israel. The chapter says that Israel, too, could become devoted to destruction, verse 26, and the rest of the story shows that Israel did come under the curse. The New Testament presents Jesus as the one who takes that curse. Paul writes that 'Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us,' Galatians 3:13. The judgment Israel deserved for following other gods, and that every idolater deserves, falls on Him.

It leads to Christ by election. Verses 7 and 8 are among the clearest statements in the Old Testament that God's choosing rests on His love, not on the worth of the chosen. The New Testament says believers were chosen 'in Him,' Ephesians 1:4, and that Christ 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for Himself a people for His own possession,' Titus 2:14, the very language of verses 6 and 8. Israel was redeemed from Pharaoh; the church is redeemed from sin by Christ's own self giving.

It leads to Christ by contrast. When James and John wanted to call down fire on a Samaritan village, Jesus rebuked them, Luke 9:54-55. When Peter drew a sword, Jesus said His kingdom is not of this world, John 18:36. He taught His followers to love their enemies and pray for their persecutors, Matthew 5:44. None of this denies the justice of Deuteronomy 7; it shows that in this age God's justice is held back so that mercy can go out to the nations, Romans 2:4.

The Christian reading needs honesty. The New Testament does not treat the Canaanite wars as an allegory of the Christian life in every detail. What it does is carry forward their two real themes: God's uncompromising hostility to idolatry, and His undeserved love for a people He chooses. Both meet at the cross, where judgment and love are fully revealed, and where Rahab's story becomes the gospel's pattern: an outsider under judgment, saved by faith in the God of Israel.
study.god:
The chapter shows God's love and God's judgment side by side, and it refuses to let either cancel the other. His love for Israel is freely given. 'The LORD did not set His affection on you ... because you were more numerous,' verse 7; He loved them 'because the LORD loved you,' verse 8. The reason for His love is His love. That circular statement is deliberate. God's love is not drawn out by anything in its object; it springs from His own nature, as Hosea 11:1 and 11:4 later describe with the image of a father leading a child with cords of kindness.

He is faithful. Verse 9 calls Him 'the faithful God who keeps His covenant of loving devotion for a thousand generations,' echoing Deuteronomy 5:10 and Exodus 20:6. He had sworn an oath to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, and the exodus happened because He kept it, verse 8. His faithfulness is the anchor of Israel's confidence as they face nations 'larger and stronger' than themselves.

He is just, and His justice is personal. He repays those who hate Him 'to their faces,' verse 10, and He will not hesitate. The judgment on Canaan is not presented as divine favouritism but as judgment on real wickedness, as Leviticus 18:24-25 and Deuteronomy 9:5 make plain. The same justice applies to Israel. The anger that would fall on Canaan will burn against Israel if they turn to other gods, verse 4. God has no double standard.

He is holy. Israel is 'a people holy to the LORD,' verse 6, and holiness is the reason for the separation the chapter demands. Idols are 'detestable to the LORD,' verse 25. God is not indifferent to what His people worship. Because He alone is God, verse 9, every rival is a lie, and His holiness will not share His people with lies.

He is sovereign in history. He 'drives out' the nations, verse 1; He has 'delivered them over,' verse 2; He sends the hornet, verse 20; He decides the pace, 'little by little,' verse 22, for the good of the land and its people. Victory depends on Him, as Psalm 44:3 later confesses: 'it was not by their sword that they took the land.'

He is patient. The judgment of Canaan waited four generations, Genesis 15:16, and in the New Testament Paul speaks of 'the riches of His kindness, tolerance, and patience,' which lead to repentance, Romans 2:4. The chapter holds a severe word, but it also shows that God's judgment is neither hasty nor arbitrary. For worship, it calls believers to marvel that they were loved before they were lovely, to take idols seriously, and to leave judgment in the hands of the faithful God.

crossReferences.note: God told Abraham his descendants would return in the fourth generation, 'for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete.' The judgment of Deuteronomy 7 is therefore not sudden or arbitrary but the end of a long patience, and it is judgment for sin, not for ethnicity.

Moses forbids Israel to think the land is a reward for their righteousness. It is given because of the nations' wickedness and to keep God's oath to the patriarchs. Read with 7:7-8, it shuts off every ground for Israel's pride in their election or their victory.

Restates the command to devote the cities of the land to destruction and names its purpose: 'so that they cannot teach you to do all the detestable things they do for their gods.' It confirms that the command concerned religious corruption and applied to these cities, not to all warfare.

At Jericho, the first city under the ban, Rahab and her household are spared because she trusted Israel's God. The exception shows that faith could bring a Canaanite out from under judgment and into Israel, an early picture of the gospel's reach.

Achan takes the devoted silver and gold and confesses, 'I coveted them and took them.' His story is Deuteronomy 7:25-26 enacted: the devoted thing brought home makes an Israelite himself devoted to destruction.

Solomon's foreign wives come from the nations about which the LORD said, 'You must not intermarry with them, for surely they will turn your hearts after their gods.' The warning of Deuteronomy 7:3-4 comes true in Israel's wisest king.

The northern kingdom falls because Israel worshipped other gods and walked in the customs of the nations the LORD had driven out. The threat of Deuteronomy 7:4 and 7:26 is carried out, showing that God judged His own people by the same standard.

Peter gives the church Israel's titles from Exodus 19:5-6 and Deuteronomy 7:6: chosen, holy, God's own possession. He adds that they were once 'not a people' and had not received mercy, so the new people, like the old, exist by grace alone.

Christ gave Himself to redeem us and to purify 'a people for His own possession.' Paul uses the Greek phrase by which the Septuagint rendered segullah in Deuteronomy 7:6, and joins it, as Moses did, to the language of redemption.

James and John want to call down fire on a Samaritan village, and Jesus rebukes them. The episode shows that Christ's disciples may not take up the judgments of Israel's conquest against those who reject them.

Paul describes the church's warfare as spiritual: weapons with divine power to demolish strongholds and tear down every argument raised against the knowledge of God. The tearing down of altars in Deuteronomy 7:5 becomes the overthrow of false ideas by truth.

'No longer will there be any curse.' The verse echoes Zechariah 14:11, where the word is the one used for the ban of Deuteronomy 7. In the new creation nothing remains under the ban, because evil has been judged and God's people dwell with Him.

study.oneStory:
Deuteronomy 7 belongs to a long story of God's judgment on evil and His mercy toward a chosen people for the sake of the world. From the flood onward, Scripture shows God judging human wickedness, and from Abraham onward it shows Him choosing one family through whom 'all the families of the earth will be blessed,' Genesis 12:3. The land of Canaan was promised to Abraham, but Genesis 15:16 said it would wait until the iniquity of its inhabitants was complete. Deuteronomy 7 is that moment arriving. It answers from before the question of how God's promise and God's justice would meet in one land.

It also sets up much of what follows. Israel was to be holy in the land, but the books of Joshua, Judges and Kings show the nations remaining and their gods becoming a snare, Judges 2:1-3. Israel intermarried, served Baal and Asherah, and finally suffered what verse 4 warned: the anger of the LORD burning against them, and exile. The chapter's warning that Israel could be 'set apart for destruction,' verse 26, came true. The chosen people proved that election does not exempt anyone from judgment.

The story's resolution comes in Christ, who bears the curse in His own body, Galatians 3:13, so that judgment and mercy meet at the cross. The treasured people of verse 6 now include those from every nation, 1 Peter 2:9-10. The warfare continues, but it is no longer against flesh and blood, Ephesians 6:12. The Rahabs of the world are welcomed by faith, and the gospel goes to every nation that once lay under judgment.

The new creation brings the chapter's themes to their final form. Evil will be judged completely and justly by Christ, Revelation 19:11, and those who cling to idols will have no place in the city, Revelation 21:8. Yet the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it, and its gates will never be shut, Revelation 21:24-25. And there will be no more ban: 'No longer will there be any curse,' Revelation 22:3. What Deuteronomy 7 pictured in a limited, historical and painful way will be fulfilled in a world where nothing detestable remains, and where a people chosen by love from every nation worship the faithful God forever.

sermon.title: Grace, Therefore, Holy
sermon.why: Keller preaches directly on Deuteronomy 7:6-11, showing that Israel's calling to holiness and separation flows entirely from grace already received, not from merit, a crucial framework for reading this chapter's hardest commands honestly.

quiz.q: Why did the LORD choose Israel, according to verses 7-8?

options.text: Not because of their size or merit, but because He loved them and kept His oath to their fathers.
options.note: Verses 7-8 state this explicitly, ruling out size or merit as the reason.

options.text: Because they were the largest and strongest of all the nations.
options.note: Verse 7 explicitly says the opposite, that they were the fewest of all peoples.

options.text: Because Israel had already earned it through perfect obedience.
options.note: The text grounds the choice in God's love and oath, not in Israel's prior obedience.

options.text: No reason at all is given for God's choice.
options.note: Verses 7-8 give an explicit, twofold reason.

quiz.q: What does Moses instruct Israel to do to the altars, pillars, and idols of the nations (v.5)?

options.text: Tear them down, smash them, cut them down, and burn them in the fire.
options.note: Verse 5 lists these exact actions against every form of Canaanite worship object.

options.text: Preserve them carefully as historical artifacts.
options.note: The instruction is total destruction, the opposite of preservation.

options.text: Sell them to neighboring nations for silver and gold.
options.note: Verse 25 explicitly forbids taking silver or gold from these objects for personal gain.

options.text: Nothing is instructed regarding these objects.
options.note: Verse 5 gives explicit, detailed instructions.

quiz.q: What promise does Moses give regarding Israel's health and fertility if they obey (vv.12-15)?

options.text: The LORD will love, bless, and multiply them, and remove sickness so there is no barren man, woman, or animal among them.
options.note: Verses 13-15 describe these specific blessings of fruitfulness and health.

options.text: They would never need to work the land again.
options.note: The blessing described is abundance and fruitfulness through the land, not an absence of labor.

options.text: They would be exempt from all future warfare.
options.note: The chapter's larger context is precisely about warfare against the nations in the land, not exemption from it.

options.text: No promise regarding health or blessing is given.
options.note: Verses 12-15 give an extensive, specific promise.

quiz.q: According to verse 22, how would the LORD drive out the nations from the land?

options.text: Little by little, so that wild animals would not overrun the land too quickly.
options.note: Verse 22 gives this exact reasoning for a gradual conquest.

options.text: Instantly, in a single day.
options.note: The text specifically describes a gradual process, not an instant one.

options.text: Through a plague that Israel itself would carry.
options.note: No such mechanism is described; verse 20 mentions the LORD sending the hornet, not a plague carried by Israel.

options.text: The text says the nations would never actually be driven out.
options.note: Verses 22-24 describe their eventual, complete removal, only gradually rather than all at once.

quiz.q: What warning does Moses give about silver and gold found on idols (v.25)?

options.text: Not to covet or take it, since it is detestable and would ensnare them.
options.note: Verse 25 gives this explicit warning against taking idols' precious metals.

options.text: To melt it down and give it entirely to the priests.
options.note: No such instruction is given; the command is to avoid taking it at all.

options.text: To keep it as spoils of war for personal wealth.
options.note: The verse explicitly forbids this, calling it a snare and something detestable.

options.text: No warning is given about idols' silver and gold.
options.note: Verse 25 gives an explicit and specific warning.

questions: Israel was chosen not because of size or merit but purely because God loved them. Where do you still tie your worth or belonging to God to your own performance rather than to His love?

This chapter's command belongs to a specific, bounded moment in redemptive history; the New Testament redirects God's people to spiritual warfare against sin and evil, never violence against people. What idols in your own heart need to be torn down and burned rather than quietly tolerated?
Moses warns Israel not to be ensnared by the silver and gold on Canaanite idols. Where might something outwardly valuable actually be entangling you with something spiritually harmful?
God said He would drive out the nations 'little by little.' Where do you need patience with a slow, gradual work of God in your life rather than expecting instant transformation?
Israel is called 'a people holy to the LORD, His treasured possession' purely by grace. How does knowing you are treasured, rather than merely tolerated, by God change how you see yourself today?

translationNotes.note: 'Devote to complete destruction' translates cherem, an irrevocable setting-apart for judgment; Genesis 15:16 frames this as judgment on the Amorites' accumulated iniquity, a bounded moment in redemptive history rather than a timeless warfare ethic.
'Treasured possession' translates segullah, a term used elsewhere for a king's personal treasure, expressing God's intimate valuing of Israel rather than mere political usefulness.

'Covenant of loving devotion' renders chesed, a word combining steadfast love and faithfulness, describing God's unwavering commitment to His promises across generations, grounded in His own character rather than Israel's merit.
